_comment: The RBAC contract: ONE answer key, four frameworks. Feature 138.
Authorization guards on top of the existing JWT auth. Two guards read the
VERIFIED token payload: role(...) checks the `roles` claim, can(...) checks the
`permissions` claim. Claim-first and zero-dependency - no DB in the v1 core. See
STATUS: OWED in all four - greenfield. No framework ships role()/can() yet, so
every invariant carries `cases: []` with the real case names parked in
`proposed_cases` and the intended per-language suite files in `proposed_suites`.
scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py therefore reports these as OWED (declared, not
yet proven) rather than FAIL. This is the pre-implementation oracle: the contract
is authored BEFORE any code, per PORTING-FORMULA.md (audit -> neutral contract ->
To implement a framework: create the named suite file, write a test per
proposed_case name (same name in every language's own idiom - the audit
normalises snake_case / testPascalCase / it-description / assert-label), move that
framework into `suites` and the names into `cases`. Real HS256 tokens via Auth,
real Request pipeline, real route dispatch - NO MOCKS. Flip owed -> proven only
when all four carry the case.

invariants.rule: A route guarded by role("admin") runs its handler when the request carries a valid token whose `roles` claim includes "admin". The subject's roles come from the verified JWT payload.
invariants.why: The positive case proves the guard reads the roles claim and lets an authorised subject through, rather than blanket-denying.

invariants.rule: A valid, authenticated token that LACKS the required role is rejected with 403 (authenticated but forbidden), not 401 and not 200. The handler never runs.
invariants.why: 403-not-200 is the whole point; 403-not-401 distinguishes 'you may not' from 'who are you'. A wrong status here breaks client behaviour and can leak resource existence.

invariants.rule: A guarded route with NO token or an INVALID/expired token returns 401 (unauthenticated), not 403. A guard implies @secured, so even a guarded GET requires authentication first.
invariants.why: Missing auth must read as 401 so clients re-authenticate; returning 403 conflates 'not logged in' with 'not allowed' and defeats standard auth flows. Proves the guard runs auth before authorization.

invariants.rule: role("admin", "editor") passes when the subject holds EITHER "admin" OR "editor" (OR within one guard). Stacking role("admin") + can("billing.read") requires BOTH (AND across guards). A subject with neither listed role is 403.
invariants.why: Pins the OR-within / AND-by-stacking semantics so a route's access set means the same thing in every framework and is not silently AND in one and OR in another.

invariants.rule: can("posts.delete") runs the handler when the token's `permissions` claim contains "posts.delete", and returns 403 when it does not. can() reads `permissions`; role() reads `roles`; the two are independent claims and the core never expands a role into permissions.
invariants.why: Proves permission checks are a distinct axis from roles, and that a role alone does not satisfy a permission guard (no implicit expansion in v1).
proposed_cases: role alone does not satisfy a permission guard

invariants.rule: A GRANTED permission "posts.*" satisfies a required "posts.delete"; a granted bare "*" satisfies every can(); a granted "posts.*" does NOT satisfy a required "users.delete". Wildcards live only on the granted side; the required permission is always concrete.
invariants.why: Wildcard on the grant side lets a token carry "posts.*" instead of enumerating every action, while a concrete requirement keeps each route's need explicit. The negative (posts.* vs users.delete) proves the boundary is dot-segment scoped, not a substring match.

invariants.rule: Roles and permissions are read ONLY from the verified JWT payload. A request that sets a spoofed header (e.g. X-Role: admin) or query param with no matching signed claim is rejected 403. An unsigned or wrongly-signed token grants nothing.
invariants.why: The obvious privilege escalation is to assert a role outside the signed token. This closes it: authorization trusts only what the validator verified.

invariants.rule: A payload carrying a singular `role: "admin"` string (the shape in current docs) is read as `roles: ["admin"]`, so role("admin") passes. Only this one legacy shape is coerced; no other legacy claim is invented.
invariants.why: Existing apps mint tokens with a singular `role`. Coercing it keeps those tokens working the day RBAC ships, so the feature is additive and non-breaking.
